title: What Actually Happens When You Open a Link
subtitle: You tap a link and a page appears. In between, your request crosses the planet and back through a dozen machines — in under a second.
hook: Tap a link and a page appears so fast it feels instant. But in that fraction of a second, your device found a specific computer somewhere on Earth, negotiated a conversation with it, and streamed a page back — hopping through routers across oceans. It's the most-used piece of engineering in history, and almost nobody knows how it works. Today: the journey of a single click.

sections.heading: Step 1: find the address (DNS)
sections.body: You typed a *name* (example.com), but computers route by *numbers* (IP addresses). So first your device asks the **DNS** — the internet's phone book — 'what's the number for this name?' It answers something like 93.184.216.34. Names are for humans; numbers are for routing.

sections.heading: Step 2: chop it into packets and route them
sections.body: Your request is broken into small **packets**, each stamped with the destination address. Routers pass each packet hop-by-hop toward its target — no single wire connects you to the server; the network figures out a path, packet by packet, and can reroute around failures. At the destination they're reassembled in order (that's **TCP**'s job: reliable, in-order delivery over an unreliable network). The server then sends the page back the same way.

sections.caption: Name → number (DNS), then your request travels as packets hopping router-to-router to the server and back.

sections.label: Why 'packets' is genius
sections.body: Splitting data into independently-routed packets is what makes the internet robust. Lose one? Resend just that one. A cable gets cut? Packets take another path. No central switchboard has to hold a dedicated line open for your whole session. This decentralized, packet-switched design is why the internet survives failures that would kill a phone-style network.

sections.caption: How data packets actually travel — routers, DNS, and the path across the internet.

takeaways: **DNS** translates the human name into a machine IP address (the internet's phone book).
Your request is split into **packets**, each routed independently toward the destination.
**TCP** reassembles packets in order and resends any that are lost — reliable delivery over an unreliable net.
No dedicated wire connects you to the server; routers find a path hop-by-hop.
Packet-switching makes the internet **robust** — it reroutes around cuts and failures.
